strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: obtaining continuous invariant predictions while retaining flexible, symmetry-unrestricted backbones. Class-specific transformation optimization provides an intuitive construction applicable to both spectral graphs and point clouds.

For continuous backbones and exact maximization over compact group orbits, the continuity and invariance arguments are convincing. The nonexpansiveness of the maximum operator also provides a clean route to universal approximation.

The experiments cover several complementary settings and report consistent improvements. Examples include 91.7% ModelNet40 accuracy for AC-DGCNN versus 90.2% for VN-DGCNN, and improvements across the five TU datasets and three OGB benchmarks. The sampling/refinement ablation and rotation-shift evaluation provide useful additional evidence.
weaknesses: The practical algorithm is not covered by the central guarantees. The theory assumes global maximization, whereas the implementation uses random candidates and a few local optimization steps. This generally does not ensure samplewise invariance or preserve the exact maximum's continuity guarantee. No optimization-error bounds, measured invariance errors, or input-perturbation stability experiments establish how closely the implementation satisfies the paper's central claims. DGCNN's discrete neighborhood selection also requires qualification when invoking continuous-backbone results.

Theorem 12(2) is false under Definition 11 for general P: its proof establishes orbit invariance, but not factorization through P. For example, take two finite orbits {a,b} and {c,d}, with P(a)=P(c)=0, P(b)=1, P(d)=2, and f(t)=t on K={0,1,2}. Orbit maximization gives outputs 1 and 2 on the respective orbits, so no single F(P(g)) can represent both outputs at a and c. This invalidates the claimed equivalence of function classes in the stated generality, although the compact identity-P setting remains viable.

The graph continuity claim has a substantially narrower scope than the motivation suggests. Section 3.1 assigns infinite distance between inputs with different spectral-band dimensions, while hard band indicators can change under arbitrarily small graph perturbations. Continuity in that constructed space does not establish stability with respect to ordinary adjacency or Laplacian perturbations. Appendix E.1 also incorrectly states that arbitrary orthogonal transformations within a spectral band commute with L; this holds within a repeated-eigenvalue eigenspace, not a band containing distinct eigenvalues.

Novelty needs stronger positioning. With strictly increasing priors, the proposed output is simply classwise maximum pooling over transformation orbits; the prior does not change the maximizer. The paper does not adequately distinguish its contribution from transformation-search and group-pooling approaches. Appendix A.2 also inaccurately characterizes frame averaging as using transformations independent of the input, weakening the comparison with existing methods.

Essential implementation and efficiency details are missing. The manuscript does not specify the actual candidate counts, refinement steps, inner-loop learning rates, or orthogonality-preserving optimization procedure. Spectral band and padding configurations are also insufficiently specified. Despite requiring optimization for every class, no measured training time, inference latency, or memory usage supports the efficiency claims; Table 5 reports only accuracy. Appendix F's softmax/cross-entropy description also conflicts with the proposed independent sigmoid/BCE formulation.

The evaluation does not sufficiently isolate the proposed mechanism. Several baseline results are imported from prior work without matched compute or tuning budgets, and ModelNet40 results lack uncertainty estimates. Missing controls include matched-budget transformation averaging/max pooling and the same backbone trained with the same one-versus-rest loss without adaptive refinement. There is also no direct evidence that gains arise from improved continuity or stability, rather than additional inference computation and changed training objectives.

This matters because optimization scales with the number of output classes, including 128 molecular prediction tasks.

For exact orbit maximization with identity priors and continuous backbones, the nonexpansiveness and continuity arguments are clear and useful. The universal approximation transfer is straightforward under the stated approximation assumptions.

The reported empirical improvements span several settings. A-NLSF achieves 73.01% on ENZYMES versus 65.94% for NLSF, and AC-DGCNN achieves 91.7% on rotated ModelNet40 versus 90.2% for VN-DGCNN. The appendix also includes sampling-versus-refinement ablations and rotation distribution-shift experiments.

For a finite space {a,b,c}, let the group swap a and b while fixing c, set P(a)=P(c)=0 and P(b)=1, and take f(0)=0, f(1)=1. Orbit maximization gives Q(a)=1 and Q(c)=0, so no F can satisfy Q=F∘P. All spaces can be compact and discrete. This invalidates the claimed characterization, although the narrower approximation transfer can survive.

The practical method does not inherit the main guarantees automatically. Finite random candidates plus local refinement need not find global maxima or produce exactly invariant predictions. The paper provides neither approximation-error guarantees nor measurements of invariance error or perturbation stability. Moreover, DGCNN's changing k-nearest-neighbor graphs can violate the continuous-backbone assumption.

The claimed graph continuity requires qualification. The analysis uses supplied spectral bases and separates different band dimensions by infinite distance; it does not establish continuity with respect to the original graph Laplacian when eigenvalues cross hard band boundaries. Appendix E.1 also incorrectly states that arbitrary orthogonal transformations within spectral bands commute with L; this holds within a single eigenspace, not generally across distinct eigenvalues.

Runtime and memory measurements are particularly important because optimization scales with the number of output classes or tasks.

strengths: The paper addresses an important limitation of canonicalization: discontinuous canonical representatives can produce unstable predictions. Maximizing each output separately provides a clear mechanism for obtaining continuous invariant scores under suitable assumptions.

The exact-max construction has useful properties: the maximum is nonexpansive in the backbone’s uniform norm, and continuity and universal approximation follow naturally in the compact group-action setting with identity preprocessing.

The empirical study is broad, covering graph classification, molecular benchmarks, point clouds, and supplementary applications. Reported improvements are consistent, and the appendix includes sampling/refinement, spectral partition, backbone, and runtime ablations.
weaknesses: Theorem 12(2) is false at the stated generality. Definition 11 requires the output to factor through P via a single continuous F, whereas the proof establishes only group invariance. For example, take two two-point orbits whose P-images are {a,b} and {a,c}, with f(a)=0, f(b)=1, and f(c)=2. Orbit maximization gives outputs 1 and 2, but Definition 11 would require F(a) to equal both. All spaces can be finite and compact. Additional conditions on P or a revised definition are necessary; the claimed characterization of the function space is therefore unsupported.

The exact guarantees do not establish the advertised properties of the implemented system. Experiments use 32 or 50 random transformations followed by local refinement, which need not achieve global maxima or exact invariance for an individual prediction. Appendix E.2 provides a pointwise sampling argument, but does not establish uniform approximation across inputs or quantify invariance errors at the actual budgets. The epoch-to-epoch rotation plot measures a different property from continuity under input perturbations.

Continuity assumptions are not verified for important applications. Hard spectral band boundaries can make graph preprocessing discontinuous when eigenvalues cross a boundary; assigning different band dimensions infinite distance does not establish stability under small adjacency perturbations. Likewise, DGCNN’s hard nearest-neighbor selection does not generally define a continuous backbone. These limitations substantially narrow the practical interpretation of the central continuity claim.

The methodological novelty needs stronger positioning against transformation-wise max pooling and latent transformation optimization. With strictly increasing priors, the predictor is simply a coordinatewise maximum over transformed backbone outputs, and the main continuity and approximation arguments are elementary properties of this operation. The discussion distinguishes learned canonicalization and averaging, but does not sufficiently establish what is new relative to max-based invariant pooling. Also, Theorem 8 needs strictly monotone priors or an appropriate tie rule: a merely monotone prior with plateaus does not justify arbitrary maximizer selection.

The comparisons do not adequately isolate the source of improvement. Important controls include identical-backbone, identical-loss comparisons using transformation averaging versus maximization at matched evaluation budgets. For the graph construction, bandwise Gram matrices C_k^T C_k characterize the orthogonal orbits at fixed band dimensions and provide a particularly relevant direct invariant baseline. Many OGB and point-cloud results are imported from prior work, and several reported margins are modest relative to their variability.

Reproducibility and efficiency evidence are incomplete. The refinement step count, step sizes, gradient treatment, and selected spectral configurations are insufficiently specified; Appendix F also describes softmax cross-entropy without clearly reconciling it with the proposed binary-cross-entropy objective. Runtime comparisons cover only small TU datasets, omitting point-cloud and OGB inference latency, peak memory, preprocessing cost, and scaling with the number of classes.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: obtaining continuous invariant predictions while retaining flexible, non-equivariant backbones. For continuous scalar predictors and exact maximization over compact group orbits, the continuity and invariance arguments are clear and useful.

The reported empirical results are promising across graph and point-cloud classification. A-NLSF improves over the listed baselines on all five TU datasets and three OGB benchmarks; AC-DGCNN reaches 91.6% on rotated ModelNet40.

The appendix provides substantial additional evaluation, including sampling-versus-refinement ablations, alternative backbones, rotation distribution shifts, spectral design choices, and graph training-time comparisons.
weaknesses: Theorem 12(2) is false under Definition 11 for general preprocessing P. Its proof establishes group invariance, but not the required factorization through P. For example, let G be the closed unit disk, let SO(2) act by rotations, let P(x,y)=x, and take f(t)=t on K=[-1,1]. Exact prior maximization returns sqrt(x²+y²), which is continuous and invariant but cannot equal F(P(x,y)): (0,0) and (0,1) have identical P values and different outputs. This invalidates the claimed characterization in the general framework, although the restricted identity-preprocessing case remains viable.

The implemented method does not inherit the exact theory automatically. Searching 32 or 50 random transformations followed by local refinement does not guarantee samplewise invariance or global maximization. Appendix E.2 supplies a generic concentration inequality, but does not instantiate its constants or establish uniform approximation for the actual search procedure. Selecting one candidate before refinement also requires a separate continuity argument. Direct measurements of prediction variation under rotations, eigenbasis changes, and small input perturbations are missing; tracking canonical rotations across training epochs does not test these properties.

The graph continuity claim has a narrower scope than the presentation suggests. Hard spectral bands can change discontinuously when eigenvalues cross band boundaries, while the proposed metric assigns infinite distance between configurations with different band dimensions. Continuity in this constructed space therefore does not establish stability to small changes in graph edge weights. Likewise, DGCNN's discrete nearest-neighbor selection is not generally a continuous backbone, so the strongest point-cloud implementation needs additional qualification.

The novelty is insufficiently distinguished from output-wise max pooling over transformation orbits. With the identity prior used experimentally, the predictor is exactly max_u f_d(κ_u(g)); its continuity and approximation properties follow from standard properties of maxima. The paper discusses energy-based canonicalization extensively, but should position this central operation against transformation pooling and isolate what the adaptive-canonicalization formalism adds beyond that operation. Appendix A.2 also incorrectly describes frame averaging as necessarily using input-independent transformations.

The comparisons do not adequately isolate the source of the gains. Important controls include the same backbone and one-vs-rest objective with compute-matched transformation averaging or max pooling, and graph predictors using bandwise Gram matrices C_kᵀC_k, which capture invariants under the full orthogonal band actions. Several OGB and ModelNet40 results are imported from prior work, limiting control over training and tuning budgets. The appendix's graph timing table is useful, but point-cloud inference latency and memory costs remain unreported despite the substantial transformation search.

Reproduction of the central algorithm remains difficult. The local-refinement step count, step size, projection choice, differentiation treatment, and final spectral band/truncation settings are not specified sufficiently. Appendix F describes softmax cross-entropy for graph experiments, whereas the main method and Appendix E prescribe summed binary cross-entropies over independently maximized outputs. This discrepancy matters because the training objective is central to the proposed construction.

strengths: The paper addresses an important limitation of canonicalization: discontinuous choices of representatives can produce unstable predictions. Maximizing each output separately gives a simple, useful construction whose exact maximum is continuous under the stated equicontinuity assumptions.
The framework accommodates ordinary backbones and has concrete applications to spectral graph representations and rotation-invariant point cloud classification.
Reported results are consistently positive across several benchmarks, including 73.01% on ENZYMES, 0.2968 average precision on ogbg-molpcba, and 91.6% on ModelNet40 with AC-DGCNN.

The appendix provides substantial additional evidence, including sampling versus refinement comparisons, spectral partition and backbone ablations, rotation distribution shifts, and training costs on TUDataset.
weaknesses: Theorem 12(2) is false at the stated generality. Its proof establishes invariance on G, but Definition 11 additionally requires factorization through P. For a finite space with two orbits {a,b} and {c,d}, take P(a)=P(c)=0, P(b)=1, P(d)=2, and f(t)=t. Orbit maximization gives outputs 1 and 2 on the two orbits, although P(a)=P(c), so no F satisfying Definition 11 exists. All spaces can be finite and compact. Additional assumptions on P are necessary; the claimed characterization of the function class is therefore unsupported, although the identity-P case and the forward approximation argument remain useful.

The practical algorithm does not inherit the headline exact guarantees. Maximization over 32 or 50 sampled transformations followed by local refinement does not establish exact invariance, and continuity of the refined output needs separate analysis. Appendix E.2 gives a generic sampling bound without establishing useful constants or uniform control for the implemented networks and transformation spaces. Repeated-rotation consistency and input-perturbation tests are missing; stabilization across training epochs does not measure these properties.

Continuity of the actual application pipelines is insufficiently justified. Hard spectral bands can change membership under arbitrarily small graph perturbations; placing different band dimensions in separate galaxies excludes these transitions rather than resolving them. DGCNN's discrete nearest-neighbor selection also need not define a continuous backbone. Thus the abstract continuity result does not establish the broad stability claims for the evaluated models.

The novelty relative to group max pooling and transformation search is not sufficiently established. With strictly increasing priors, the classifier is simply coordinatewise maximization over transformed inputs. Its nonexpansiveness and invariant universal approximation follow directly from standard maximum-operator arguments. The paper discusses related canonicalization methods extensively but does not convincingly isolate what is new beyond this reinterpretation and the spectral application.

The comparisons do not adequately isolate the proposed mechanism. Several OGB and point cloud results are imported from prior work. Missing controls include the same backbone with the same one-versus-rest loss, transformation budget, and training protocol, comparing maximum aggregation, averaging, augmentation, and refinement. These controls are especially important because the method changes both the objective and the number of evaluated views.

Reproduction and efficiency assessment remain incomplete. Refinement step counts, learning rates, stopping rules, and differentiation details are not specified sufficiently. Appendix F describes softmax cross-entropy where Appendix E specifies summed binary cross-entropies, leaving the actual training objective ambiguous. Timing is limited to small graph datasets, without inference latency or memory measurements for ModelNet40 and large OGB tasks, where per-class optimization is particularly consequential.
